medical.title: Proning and high-frequency oscillation may not reduce duration of ventilation for children with lung injury
medical.summary: A treatment that is part of standard care for adults with acute respiratory distress syndrome does not provide the same benefit in children. Children with severe acute lung injury placed in the prone position do not spend less time dependent on a ventilator. High-frequency oscillatory ventilation does not shorten the duration of mechanical ventilation either. This is shown by a worldwide study led, among others, by UMCG pediatric intensivist Dr. Martin Kneyber. The results were published in The Lancet.

medical.title: What science says about perimenopause, menopause and mood swings—minus the hype
medical.summary: After decades of relative neglect, menopause is suddenly everywhere—in the news, on social media and in conversations among friends. Some are calling it the "meno-boom," and booms attract business.

medical.title: AI improves questionnaire-based Parkinson's screening while working around missing answers
medical.summary: Scientists at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI) have developed an artificial intelligence model to streamline and improve screening for Parkinson's disease (PD) so doctors can refer patients for early-stage testing.

medical.title: New drug-development strategy might protect neurons by displacing proteins that inhibit helpful enzymes
medical.summary: Researchers from the University of California, Berkeley may have discovered a new strategy for treating complex neurodegenerative diseases. Their study, recently published in Science, describes a new approach that allows specialized enzymes to clear out several disease-causing proteins. So far, the method has proved useful for protecting neurons in lab tests.

medical.title: How your brain learned to love coffee, chocolate, fat and sugar
medical.summary: If you can remember your first sip of coffee, the memory might not be a pleasant one. Coffee's bitter flavor is one we naturally steer clear of. So how do coffee fans learn to love it? The answer may lie in an understudied "slow" dopamine pathway connecting the gut and brain. A new study from UC San Francisco shows that this pathway helps the brain connect a flavor with the beneficial effects that follow ingesting it.

medical.title: Stair climbers are said to boost fitness, strength and bone health—here's what the evidence actually says
medical.summary: The stair climber has seen a huge surge in popularity on social media in recent years. Proponents of the exercise machine rave about its benefits—claiming it can boost cardiovascular fitness, strength and bone health.

medical.title: Researchers identify genetic 'convergence' in autism and a possible explanation for the female protective effect
medical.summary: In many cases, all it takes is one mutated gene to orchestrate changes across a whole network of genes linked to autism, according to new results published in Nature by researchers at Boston Children's Hospital. The finding could explain why different mutations in one or several of the hundreds of genes linked to autism can lead to a similar condition.

medical.title: Drawings of near-death experiences reveal patterns in what people remember seeing
medical.summary: For people who have near-death experiences (NDEs), these encounters can be so deeply moving and life-changing that language seems inadequate. Many describe them as vivid, multisensory experiences, filled with mental imagery of colors, places and people.

medical.title: Lung antibodies can be measured in exhaled breath
medical.summary: For the first time, researchers have successfully measured antibodies against specific respiratory viruses in exhaled air. The new study, involving the Karolinska Institutet, was published in eBioMedicine. The method may make it easier to study the immune system in the small airways of the lungs.

medical.title: Digital therapy offers new way to prevent worsening anxiety around childbirth
medical.summary: Pregnant women with undiagnosed anxiety could benefit from a new digital therapy, according to a clinical trial led by King's College London. Published in JAMA Network Open, the results from the REducing Levels of AnXiety (RELAX) study have shown that self-led digital therapy significantly reduced participants' pre- and post-birth anxiety compared with participants who received usual care.

medical.title: Collapsible bicycle helmets provide less protection on average than conventional helmets, new study finds
medical.summary: New research from Imperial College London has found that, on average, collapsible (sometimes called "foldable") bicycle helmets provide lower levels of protection against serious head injuries than noncollapsible helmets.

medical.title: Alternative pathways for blood vessel growth could become targets against drug-resistant tumors
medical.summary: Researchers at the Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III (CNIC), together with international collaborators, have uncovered previously unknown mechanisms that allow blood vessels to grow even in the absence of VEGF–VEGFR2 signaling, one of the best-known and most widely targeted pathways in clinical efforts to block tumor angiogenesis, growth and metastasis.

medical.title: Uncovering rules for aggressive brain tumors could lead to better treatments
medical.summary: Aggressive brain tumors follow predictable rules, not chaotic randomness, according to new research. This discovery could lead to new, much-needed ways to treat glioblastoma tumors in the future.

medical.title: Mice that watch fights come away battle-ready
medical.summary: People love to watch violent things. From slasher films to boxing, there's some intrinsic appeal to watching people get pummeled. The dystopian thriller "Squid Game," for instance, debuted in 2021 and in three years racked up 330 million streams totaling more than 2.8 billion hours viewed. Even monkeys pay more attention to videos of other monkeys fighting.

medical.title: Emergency surgery verification linked to lower death rates, shorter hospital stays
medical.summary: Patients treated at hospitals that earned American College of Surgeons (ACS) Emergency General Surgery Verification demonstrated lower 30-day death rates and experienced shorter hospital stays after their hospitals earned verification, according to an analysis published in JAMA Surgery. The analysis included more than 20,000 patients who underwent emergency general surgery at 55 hospitals, five of which became verified during the study period.

medical.title: Pulse oximetry–based scoring may miss sleep apnea events in Black patients
medical.summary: Sleep studies often use a pulse oximeter to determine the severity of sleep apnea. But a new study by investigators from Mass General Brigham reports that pulse oximeters may undercount breathing events in Black patients, potentially leading to inaccurate severity classifications.

medical.title: Prostate cancer drug shows promise in new clinical trial
medical.summary: In a recent Yale-led clinical trial, a new type of prostate cancer drug showed promising results in reducing tumor activity and pain for patients with metastatic prostate cancer.

medical.title: Does time on social media make teens anxious and depressed? The evidence is not so clear
medical.summary: Parents are understandably worried about the impact of social media on the mental health of their children.

medical.title: Australia is set to get a Wegovy pill. How does it compare with weight‑loss injections?
medical.summary: A new tablet version of Wegovy, a peptide used to help people lose weight, has been approved for the first time in Australia.

medical.title: AI uncovers rapid changes in Parkinson's brain signals by separating rhythms from background activity
medical.summary: A research team led by professor Ji-Woong Choi of the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at DGIST has developed NONOS, a deep learning–based analysis technology that precisely separates rhythms from the underlying background signals in brain signals with high temporal resolution. The team collaborated with research teams led by professor Han-Joon Kim of Kumoh National Institute of Technology, professor Kyong Hwan Jin of Korea University and Dr. Jong-Cheol Rah of the Korea Brain Research Institute. The findings are published in NeuroImage.

medical.title: Hydrogel could be potential treatment for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
medical.summary: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects approximately 38% of the global population, with prevalence continuing to rise in parallel with the global burden of metabolic syndrome. Although several pharmacological agents are currently under clinical investigation, approved therapeutic options remain limited in both efficacy and scope.

medical.title: A much-needed new way to inactivate GPCRs, the most common drug targets
medical.summary: About one-third of all drugs approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration target G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), a family of more than 800 cell-surface receptors that regulate a wide range of vital functions, including blood pressure, heart rate and immunity.

medical.title: A third of babies have peanut allergy diagnosis removed
medical.summary: A world-first national program has discovered more than a third of babies thought to have a peanut allergy could safely have the diagnosis removed. And the findings are changing how Australia's health care system approaches infant food allergies.

medical.title: Consuming colorful produce may help reduce COPD-related inflammation, flare-ups
medical.summary: Eating a diet rich in red, yellow and orange fruits and vegetables may help reduce inflammation and exacerbations associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), according to a new study in the September 2026 issue of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Diseases: Journal of the COPD Foundation.

medical.title: A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered a compound that transforms a natural muscle-repair protein into a more powerful version dubbed "Super HGF," more than doubling its ability to bind to a key receptor while protecting it from age-related chemical damage. The breakthrough, supported by early mouse experiments, could eventually help combat muscle loss and preserve strength as people age.

science.title: Race, age and gender associated with experiences of harassment among gig workers
science.summary: The gig economy is rapidly growing, and scholars are still working to understand the conditions gig workers encounter. Julieta Aguilar at the University of Kentucky, U.S., and Dr. Jeremy Reynolds at Purdue University, U.S., examined experiences of harassment in the gig economy. Their study, published on Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One, found associations between race, gender, age and reported experiences of harassment, indicating that already precarious employment may be even more fraught for some workers.

science.title: Some cats are shy, just like human infants
science.summary: Some cats display a complex mixture of fear and curiosity, which is similar to shyness observed in human infants, according to a study published Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Madoka Hattori at Kyoto University, Japan, and colleagues.

science.title: Big extended families help adult female ground squirrels survive hibernation
science.summary: For Belding's ground squirrels, adult females are more likely to survive from year to year if they live near more adult female kin—but neither males nor young females get the same boost from nearby family. Jill Mateo and colleagues at the University of Chicago, U.S., report these findings on Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One.

science.title: A 7,000-year-old piece of leather reveals a deep history of Spanish goats
science.summary: Ancient DNA reveals that denizens of the Iberian Peninsula made leather from domestic goats as far back as 7,000 years ago, according to a study published Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Jolijn A. M. Erven of University College Dublin, Ireland, and colleagues.

science.title: Trained dogs detected invasive plant species in Germany with 75% accuracy
science.summary: Invasive alien species (IAS) are one of the main causes of biodiversity loss worldwide. A study published Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Annegret Grimm-Seyfarth at Helmholtz-Centre for Environmental Research—UFZ, Germany, and colleagues found that with training, volunteer dog-handler teams could locate invasive species in the wild with 75% accuracy.

science.title: Scientists discover there are way more bugs in California than you thought
science.summary: A new study published in the journal Ecography finds that there are more than 60,000 different species of insects in California—and scientists have only described about two-thirds of them.

science.title: Five things to know about guiding sound for better communication
science.summary: Every time someone picks up a call, the phone does a quiet bit of translation. Incoming radio signals are converted into tiny sound waves that ripple across chips before being turned back into data.

science.title: Molecular imaging reveals how shape-shifting protein complex captures DNA and holds separate sections together
science.summary: Researchers at Kanazawa University and the National Institute of Genetics in Japan have used high-speed atomic force microscopy to observe how a group of proteins known as Smc5/6 interacts with DNA. The images reveal how this structure opens and closes, captures DNA and brings separate sections together. The researchers also observed Smc5/6 holding twisted sections of DNA in place, producing more tightly packed arrangements. The findings, published in Nature Communications, provide new insights into the molecular processes that contribute to the maintenance and repair of genetic material.

science.title: This fruit fly's aphrodisiac reveals how social and environmental context shape mating practices
science.summary: Imagine a crowded dance floor where bodies move to the beat beneath a glittering disco ball. Some of the dancers pair up, drawn together by the heady atmosphere. For flies, as for humans, the right atmosphere can serve as a potent aphrodisiac.

science.title: Overlooked Melbourne patch reveals 45 animal species and more than 40 plant types
science.summary: When we think about nature in our cities, what often comes to mind are parks and reserves—planned, managed and clearly marked spaces that support animal and plant life in our urban environment.

science.title: Fireworks provide a few minutes of joy, but the economic and environmental costs last much longer
science.summary: Every Bonfire Night, people pay for a box of fireworks so their friends and family can enjoy the colorful display. Within a few minutes, it's all over. But the price on the box doesn't reflect the hidden costs: the smoke inhaled by neighbors, the animals disturbed or the public services called out when things go wrong.

science.title: Satellites leak noise that interferes with telescopes and GPS. Here's how to fix it
science.summary: Less than a decade ago, there were about 2,000 operational satellites orbiting Earth. Today there are more than 15,000. Millions more are planned.

science.title: Nature's looking glass: Crafting mirrors from plants
science.summary: Natural materials, ranging from butterfly wings to mother-of-pearl, can exhibit an array of optical effects. In trying to reproduce these effects, scientists have found it challenging to use biodegradable, sustainable raw ingredients while also achieving the high levels of reflectivity required for certain applications.

science.title: Speaking in a second language may shift your moral compass—but it can't overpower it
science.summary: In today's interconnected world, millions of people move between two or more languages every day. They may negotiate at work in one language, speak with family in another and follow news, entertainment and social media across several others.

science.title: New species of pygmygoby discovered at the edge of the Red Sea's unexplored deep reefs
science.summary: Researchers have described a new species of fish from the northern Red Sea, found at the entrance to a cave on a steep reef slope. Charon's pygmygoby (Trimma charon) is a small, translucent fish with a broad orange-red stripe, golden spots on its tail and an unusual four-part eye. The two known specimens measure just 12 and 17 millimeters (0.47 and 0.67 inches).

science.title: NASA Navigation Experiment Shows Promise for Planetary Landings
science.summary: NASA successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the Moon and on other planets. An Alta-X drone equipped with the agency’s Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) guidance, navigation, and control payload completed simulated lunar descent and landing maneuvers Aug. 27. The flight took place […]

science.title: Intercropping could improve animal feed and reduce environmental impact
science.summary: Scientists at Nottingham Trent University, the International Centre for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) in Ethiopia and Ethiopia's Jimma University wanted to explore the benefits of growing oats and alfalfa together, as opposed to separately, and without irrigation or fertilizer. The research is published in the Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture.

science.title: Pulsars set first mass limits on supermassive black hole pairs in the early universe
science.summary: So far, observations by instruments including the James Webb Space Telescope have revealed the presence of surprisingly massive black holes in the early universe. Even less than a billion years after the Big Bang, some of these bodies already weighed billions of times the mass of the sun, and to date, astronomers are unclear as to how they could have grown so large so quickly.

science.title: NASA Space Grant Students Fuel Agency’s Inspiration Tour
science.summary: NASA’s Inspiration Tour spread the excitement of space exploration and aeronautical innovation by connecting the public, industry, and academia with the people, technologies, and organizations that drive American leadership in space. At nearly every stop across the country, NASA Space Grant has brought students into the heart of the action. In Iowa, NASA Administrator Jared […]

science.title: From ABCs to geometry: Kindergarten readiness linked to math achievement through ninth grade
science.summary: Children's developmental readiness in kindergarten can predict their math achievement as late as ninth grade, according to research from the University of Toronto's Ontario Institute for Studies in Education (OISE).

science.title: New modeling links gaps in Earth's geological record to rising and sinking continents
science.summary: Research led by a University of Wollongong (UOW) Ph.D. candidate may have solved one of Earth's most perplexing geological mysteries: What caused the Great Unconformity?

science.title: Ancient DNA traces origins of English, German and Scandinavian languages
science.summary: English, German, Dutch and the Scandinavian languages are all members of the Germanic language group, spoken by hundreds of millions of people today. But where did these languages come from?

science.title: Giant planet emerges from two-year-old JWST data thanks to glare-removal technique
science.summary: Even the world's most powerful telescopes have their blind spots. Although NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) can peer billions of years into the past, it still struggles to photograph planets orbiting nearby stars. Stars shine with such extraordinary brightness that their glare overwhelms nearby planets' faint glow.

science.title: Researchers use seasonal satellite imagery to map shrub encroachment in Inner Mongolia grasslands
science.summary: Researchers from the Aerospace Information Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (AIRCAS) used satellite images collected across the growing season to map shrub cover in the grasslands of Inner Mongolia, China. By tracking seasonal differences in growth, they were able to distinguish shrub patches from dense grass, which can look similar in a single image.

science.title: Foot-stiffening socks could make walking less tiring
science.summary: Human feet are much stiffer than those of other primates, which means they limit midfoot bending during walking. The evolutionary reasons for this are not entirely clear. One idea is that the features that stiffen the foot evolved to make upright walking less effortful.

environment.title: Suriname’s rich archaeological history may hold keys to conservation
environment.summary: Suriname pledges to save its forests but neglects the ancient human history hidden within them, experts say.

environment.title: A town-wide ‘living laboratory’ shows how green spaces can combat climate extremes
environment.summary: Stoke Park is a natural haven in a busy British town. Centered in Guildford, Surrey, its rolling fields pop with wildflowers in the spring; birds sing and ducks paddle serenely in a pond beside ornamental gardens; and the sun casts dappled shade on the grass from oak, spruce and beech trees, scattered across 52 hectares […]

environment.title: Why I sent my archive of nature’s sounds to France (commentary)
environment.summary: It is a peculiar irony: as technology reaches ever deeper into Earth’s living systems, the primal sonic expressions of the natural world—wind, water, leaf, and creature—have never been more imperiled. Soundscape ecology rests on a simple conviction: the collective voices of the nonhuman world are not only eloquent, but essential. Recorded and preserved over time, […]

environment.summary: In his second term as the U.S. president, Donald Trump has taken actions to remove protections from at least 34.8 million hectares (86 million acres) of public lands, according to the advocacy group Center for American Progress. The nonprofit Conservation Lands Foundation (CLF) recently catalogued 12 such policy actions in its newly released Public Lands […]

environment.summary: KAKINADA, India (AP) — A powerful cyclone battered India ’s Andhra Pradesh state on Wednesday, killing at least three people and damaging homes and farmland after authorities evacuated tens of thousands of people, officials said. Cyclone Arnab made landfall early Wednesday as a very severe cyclonic storm before weakening to a severe cyclonic storm as […]

environment.title: Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years
environment.summary: Switzerland’s glaciers are disappearing at an alarming rate, losing more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Some of the country’s most famous glaciers experienced their worst melting on record, while several smaller glaciers vanished completely. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.

environment.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in Japan's 7,300-year-old volcanic apocalypse
environment.summary: A catastrophic volcanic eruption 7,300 years ago devastated Japan, but new research reveals that its impact on prehistoric populations was far more complex than previously believed. While some communities disappeared or declined, others unexpectedly flourished as survivors migrated, adapted, and found new ways to thrive.

environment.title: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
environment.summary: Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.

environment.title: Europe's new Sentinel-3C satellite just sent back spectacular images of Earth
environment.summary: Europe's Sentinel-3C satellite has returned breathtaking images of Earth just two weeks after launch, revealing the snowy Alps, frozen Arctic islands, and brilliant turquoise Caribbean waters. Its first measurements also show promising results for tracking rising seas, melting ice sheets, and other changes reshaping our planet.

environment.title: Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
environment.summary: Scientists may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth maintained enough oxygen to support life. Ancient rocks reveal that phosphorus recycling in the oceans created a self-sustaining cycle that helped keep oxygen levels high, even as the planet underwent dramatic environmental changes. The discovery challenges assumptions about Earth's early atmosphere and raises new questions about why complex life took so long to emerge.

environment.title: Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
environment.summary: The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. Scientists discovered that these changes in the genome's 3D structure may have helped drive the evolution of their unusually complex nervous systems.

mix_items.title: Race, age and gender associated with experiences of harassment among gig workers
mix_items.summary: The gig economy is rapidly growing, and scholars are still working to understand the conditions gig workers encounter. Julieta Aguilar at the University of Kentucky, U.S., and Dr. Jeremy Reynolds at Purdue University, U.S., examined experiences of harassment in the gig economy. Their study, published on Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One, found associations between race, gender, age and reported experiences of harassment, indicating that already precarious employment may be even more fraught for some workers.

mix_items.title: Some cats are shy, just like human infants
mix_items.summary: Some cats display a complex mixture of fear and curiosity, which is similar to shyness observed in human infants, according to a study published Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Madoka Hattori at Kyoto University, Japan, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Big extended families help adult female ground squirrels survive hibernation
mix_items.summary: For Belding's ground squirrels, adult females are more likely to survive from year to year if they live near more adult female kin—but neither males nor young females get the same boost from nearby family. Jill Mateo and colleagues at the University of Chicago, U.S., report these findings on Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One.

mix_items.title: A 7,000-year-old piece of leather reveals a deep history of Spanish goats
mix_items.summary: Ancient DNA reveals that denizens of the Iberian Peninsula made leather from domestic goats as far back as 7,000 years ago, according to a study published Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Jolijn A. M. Erven of University College Dublin, Ireland, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Trained dogs detected invasive plant species in Germany with 75% accuracy
mix_items.summary: Invasive alien species (IAS) are one of the main causes of biodiversity loss worldwide. A study published Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Annegret Grimm-Seyfarth at Helmholtz-Centre for Environmental Research—UFZ, Germany, and colleagues found that with training, volunteer dog-handler teams could locate invasive species in the wild with 75% accuracy.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover there are way more bugs in California than you thought
mix_items.summary: A new study published in the journal Ecography finds that there are more than 60,000 different species of insects in California—and scientists have only described about two-thirds of them.

mix_items.title: Proning and high-frequency oscillation may not reduce duration of ventilation for children with lung injury
mix_items.summary: A treatment that is part of standard care for adults with acute respiratory distress syndrome does not provide the same benefit in children. Children with severe acute lung injury placed in the prone position do not spend less time dependent on a ventilator. High-frequency oscillatory ventilation does not shorten the duration of mechanical ventilation either. This is shown by a worldwide study led, among others, by UMCG pediatric intensivist Dr. Martin Kneyber. The results were published in The Lancet.

mix_items.title: Five things to know about guiding sound for better communication
mix_items.summary: Every time someone picks up a call, the phone does a quiet bit of translation. Incoming radio signals are converted into tiny sound waves that ripple across chips before being turned back into data.

mix_items.title: What science says about perimenopause, menopause and mood swings—minus the hype
mix_items.summary: After decades of relative neglect, menopause is suddenly everywhere—in the news, on social media and in conversations among friends. Some are calling it the "meno-boom," and booms attract business.

mix_items.title: Molecular imaging reveals how shape-shifting protein complex captures DNA and holds separate sections together
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Kanazawa University and the National Institute of Genetics in Japan have used high-speed atomic force microscopy to observe how a group of proteins known as Smc5/6 interacts with DNA. The images reveal how this structure opens and closes, captures DNA and brings separate sections together. The researchers also observed Smc5/6 holding twisted sections of DNA in place, producing more tightly packed arrangements. The findings, published in Nature Communications, provide new insights into the molecular processes that contribute to the maintenance and repair of genetic material.

mix_items.title: AI improves questionnaire-based Parkinson's screening while working around missing answers
mix_items.summary: Scientists at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI) have developed an artificial intelligence model to streamline and improve screening for Parkinson's disease (PD) so doctors can refer patients for early-stage testing.

mix_items.title: New drug-development strategy might protect neurons by displacing proteins that inhibit helpful enzymes
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the University of California, Berkeley may have discovered a new strategy for treating complex neurodegenerative diseases. Their study, recently published in Science, describes a new approach that allows specialized enzymes to clear out several disease-causing proteins. So far, the method has proved useful for protecting neurons in lab tests.

mix_items.title: How your brain learned to love coffee, chocolate, fat and sugar
mix_items.summary: If you can remember your first sip of coffee, the memory might not be a pleasant one. Coffee's bitter flavor is one we naturally steer clear of. So how do coffee fans learn to love it? The answer may lie in an understudied "slow" dopamine pathway connecting the gut and brain. A new study from UC San Francisco shows that this pathway helps the brain connect a flavor with the beneficial effects that follow ingesting it.

mix_items.title: Stair climbers are said to boost fitness, strength and bone health—here's what the evidence actually says
mix_items.summary: The stair climber has seen a huge surge in popularity on social media in recent years. Proponents of the exercise machine rave about its benefits—claiming it can boost cardiovascular fitness, strength and bone health.

mix_items.title: This fruit fly's aphrodisiac reveals how social and environmental context shape mating practices
mix_items.summary: Imagine a crowded dance floor where bodies move to the beat beneath a glittering disco ball. Some of the dancers pair up, drawn together by the heady atmosphere. For flies, as for humans, the right atmosphere can serve as a potent aphrodisiac.

mix_items.title: Overlooked Melbourne patch reveals 45 animal species and more than 40 plant types
mix_items.summary: When we think about nature in our cities, what often comes to mind are parks and reserves—planned, managed and clearly marked spaces that support animal and plant life in our urban environment.

mix_items.title: Researchers identify genetic 'convergence' in autism and a possible explanation for the female protective effect
mix_items.summary: In many cases, all it takes is one mutated gene to orchestrate changes across a whole network of genes linked to autism, according to new results published in Nature by researchers at Boston Children's Hospital. The finding could explain why different mutations in one or several of the hundreds of genes linked to autism can lead to a similar condition.

mix_items.title: Fireworks provide a few minutes of joy, but the economic and environmental costs last much longer
mix_items.summary: Every Bonfire Night, people pay for a box of fireworks so their friends and family can enjoy the colorful display. Within a few minutes, it's all over. But the price on the box doesn't reflect the hidden costs: the smoke inhaled by neighbors, the animals disturbed or the public services called out when things go wrong.

mix_items.title: Satellites leak noise that interferes with telescopes and GPS. Here's how to fix it
mix_items.summary: Less than a decade ago, there were about 2,000 operational satellites orbiting Earth. Today there are more than 15,000. Millions more are planned.

mix_items.title: Drawings of near-death experiences reveal patterns in what people remember seeing
mix_items.summary: For people who have near-death experiences (NDEs), these encounters can be so deeply moving and life-changing that language seems inadequate. Many describe them as vivid, multisensory experiences, filled with mental imagery of colors, places and people.

mix_items.title: Nature's looking glass: Crafting mirrors from plants
mix_items.summary: Natural materials, ranging from butterfly wings to mother-of-pearl, can exhibit an array of optical effects. In trying to reproduce these effects, scientists have found it challenging to use biodegradable, sustainable raw ingredients while also achieving the high levels of reflectivity required for certain applications.

mix_items.title: Speaking in a second language may shift your moral compass—but it can't overpower it
mix_items.summary: In today's interconnected world, millions of people move between two or more languages every day. They may negotiate at work in one language, speak with family in another and follow news, entertainment and social media across several others.

mix_items.title: Lung antibodies can be measured in exhaled breath
mix_items.summary: For the first time, researchers have successfully measured antibodies against specific respiratory viruses in exhaled air. The new study, involving the Karolinska Institutet, was published in eBioMedicine. The method may make it easier to study the immune system in the small airways of the lungs.

mix_items.title: New species of pygmygoby discovered at the edge of the Red Sea's unexplored deep reefs
mix_items.summary: Researchers have described a new species of fish from the northern Red Sea, found at the entrance to a cave on a steep reef slope. Charon's pygmygoby (Trimma charon) is a small, translucent fish with a broad orange-red stripe, golden spots on its tail and an unusual four-part eye. The two known specimens measure just 12 and 17 millimeters (0.47 and 0.67 inches).

mix_items.title: NASA Navigation Experiment Shows Promise for Planetary Landings
mix_items.summary: NASA successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the Moon and on other planets. An Alta-X drone equipped with the agency’s Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) guidance, navigation, and control payload completed simulated lunar descent and landing maneuvers Aug. 27. The flight took place […]

mix_items.title: Intercropping could improve animal feed and reduce environmental impact
mix_items.summary: Scientists at Nottingham Trent University, the International Centre for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) in Ethiopia and Ethiopia's Jimma University wanted to explore the benefits of growing oats and alfalfa together, as opposed to separately, and without irrigation or fertilizer. The research is published in the Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture.

mix_items.title: Digital therapy offers new way to prevent worsening anxiety around childbirth
mix_items.summary: Pregnant women with undiagnosed anxiety could benefit from a new digital therapy, according to a clinical trial led by King's College London. Published in JAMA Network Open, the results from the REducing Levels of AnXiety (RELAX) study have shown that self-led digital therapy significantly reduced participants' pre- and post-birth anxiety compared with participants who received usual care.

mix_items.title: Pulsars set first mass limits on supermassive black hole pairs in the early universe
mix_items.summary: So far, observations by instruments including the James Webb Space Telescope have revealed the presence of surprisingly massive black holes in the early universe. Even less than a billion years after the Big Bang, some of these bodies already weighed billions of times the mass of the sun, and to date, astronomers are unclear as to how they could have grown so large so quickly.

mix_items.title: Collapsible bicycle helmets provide less protection on average than conventional helmets, new study finds
mix_items.summary: New research from Imperial College London has found that, on average, collapsible (sometimes called "foldable") bicycle helmets provide lower levels of protection against serious head injuries than noncollapsible helmets.

mix_items.title: NASA Space Grant Students Fuel Agency’s Inspiration Tour
mix_items.summary: NASA’s Inspiration Tour spread the excitement of space exploration and aeronautical innovation by connecting the public, industry, and academia with the people, technologies, and organizations that drive American leadership in space. At nearly every stop across the country, NASA Space Grant has brought students into the heart of the action. In Iowa, NASA Administrator Jared […]

mix_items.title: Alternative pathways for blood vessel growth could become targets against drug-resistant tumors
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III (CNIC), together with international collaborators, have uncovered previously unknown mechanisms that allow blood vessels to grow even in the absence of VEGF–VEGFR2 signaling, one of the best-known and most widely targeted pathways in clinical efforts to block tumor angiogenesis, growth and metastasis.

mix_items.title: Uncovering rules for aggressive brain tumors could lead to better treatments
mix_items.summary: Aggressive brain tumors follow predictable rules, not chaotic randomness, according to new research. This discovery could lead to new, much-needed ways to treat glioblastoma tumors in the future.

mix_items.title: Mice that watch fights come away battle-ready
mix_items.summary: People love to watch violent things. From slasher films to boxing, there's some intrinsic appeal to watching people get pummeled. The dystopian thriller "Squid Game," for instance, debuted in 2021 and in three years racked up 330 million streams totaling more than 2.8 billion hours viewed. Even monkeys pay more attention to videos of other monkeys fighting.

mix_items.title: From ABCs to geometry: Kindergarten readiness linked to math achievement through ninth grade
mix_items.summary: Children's developmental readiness in kindergarten can predict their math achievement as late as ninth grade, according to research from the University of Toronto's Ontario Institute for Studies in Education (OISE).

mix_items.title: New modeling links gaps in Earth's geological record to rising and sinking continents
mix_items.summary: Research led by a University of Wollongong (UOW) Ph.D. candidate may have solved one of Earth's most perplexing geological mysteries: What caused the Great Unconformity?

mix_items.title: Ancient DNA traces origins of English, German and Scandinavian languages
mix_items.summary: English, German, Dutch and the Scandinavian languages are all members of the Germanic language group, spoken by hundreds of millions of people today. But where did these languages come from?

mix_items.title: Emergency surgery verification linked to lower death rates, shorter hospital stays
mix_items.summary: Patients treated at hospitals that earned American College of Surgeons (ACS) Emergency General Surgery Verification demonstrated lower 30-day death rates and experienced shorter hospital stays after their hospitals earned verification, according to an analysis published in JAMA Surgery. The analysis included more than 20,000 patients who underwent emergency general surgery at 55 hospitals, five of which became verified during the study period.

mix_items.title: Pulse oximetry–based scoring may miss sleep apnea events in Black patients
mix_items.summary: Sleep studies often use a pulse oximeter to determine the severity of sleep apnea. But a new study by investigators from Mass General Brigham reports that pulse oximeters may undercount breathing events in Black patients, potentially leading to inaccurate severity classifications.

mix_items.title: Giant planet emerges from two-year-old JWST data thanks to glare-removal technique
mix_items.summary: Even the world's most powerful telescopes have their blind spots. Although NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) can peer billions of years into the past, it still struggles to photograph planets orbiting nearby stars. Stars shine with such extraordinary brightness that their glare overwhelms nearby planets' faint glow.

mix_items.title: Researchers use seasonal satellite imagery to map shrub encroachment in Inner Mongolia grasslands
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the Aerospace Information Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (AIRCAS) used satellite images collected across the growing season to map shrub cover in the grasslands of Inner Mongolia, China. By tracking seasonal differences in growth, they were able to distinguish shrub patches from dense grass, which can look similar in a single image.

mix_items.title: Prostate cancer drug shows promise in new clinical trial
mix_items.summary: In a recent Yale-led clinical trial, a new type of prostate cancer drug showed promising results in reducing tumor activity and pain for patients with metastatic prostate cancer.

mix_items.title: Foot-stiffening socks could make walking less tiring
mix_items.summary: Human feet are much stiffer than those of other primates, which means they limit midfoot bending during walking. The evolutionary reasons for this are not entirely clear. One idea is that the features that stiffen the foot evolved to make upright walking less effortful.

mix_items.title: Does time on social media make teens anxious and depressed? The evidence is not so clear
mix_items.summary: Parents are understandably worried about the impact of social media on the mental health of their children.

mix_items.title: Australia is set to get a Wegovy pill. How does it compare with weight‑loss injections?
mix_items.summary: A new tablet version of Wegovy, a peptide used to help people lose weight, has been approved for the first time in Australia.

mix_items.title: AI uncovers rapid changes in Parkinson's brain signals by separating rhythms from background activity
mix_items.summary: A research team led by professor Ji-Woong Choi of the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at DGIST has developed NONOS, a deep learning–based analysis technology that precisely separates rhythms from the underlying background signals in brain signals with high temporal resolution. The team collaborated with research teams led by professor Han-Joon Kim of Kumoh National Institute of Technology, professor Kyong Hwan Jin of Korea University and Dr. Jong-Cheol Rah of the Korea Brain Research Institute. The findings are published in NeuroImage.

mix_items.title: Hydrogel could be potential treatment for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
mix_items.summary: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects approximately 38% of the global population, with prevalence continuing to rise in parallel with the global burden of metabolic syndrome. Although several pharmacological agents are currently under clinical investigation, approved therapeutic options remain limited in both efficacy and scope.

mix_items.title: A much-needed new way to inactivate GPCRs, the most common drug targets
mix_items.summary: About one-third of all drugs approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration target G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), a family of more than 800 cell-surface receptors that regulate a wide range of vital functions, including blood pressure, heart rate and immunity.

mix_items.title: A third of babies have peanut allergy diagnosis removed
mix_items.summary: A world-first national program has discovered more than a third of babies thought to have a peanut allergy could safely have the diagnosis removed. And the findings are changing how Australia's health care system approaches infant food allergies.

mix_items.title: Consuming colorful produce may help reduce COPD-related inflammation, flare-ups
mix_items.summary: Eating a diet rich in red, yellow and orange fruits and vegetables may help reduce inflammation and exacerbations associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), according to a new study in the September 2026 issue of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Diseases: Journal of the COPD Foundation.

mix_items.title: A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a compound that transforms a natural muscle-repair protein into a more powerful version dubbed "Super HGF," more than doubling its ability to bind to a key receptor while protecting it from age-related chemical damage. The breakthrough, supported by early mouse experiments, could eventually help combat muscle loss and preserve strength as people age.

mix_items.title: Suriname’s rich archaeological history may hold keys to conservation
mix_items.summary: Suriname pledges to save its forests but neglects the ancient human history hidden within them, experts say.

mix_items.title: A town-wide ‘living laboratory’ shows how green spaces can combat climate extremes
mix_items.summary: Stoke Park is a natural haven in a busy British town. Centered in Guildford, Surrey, its rolling fields pop with wildflowers in the spring; birds sing and ducks paddle serenely in a pond beside ornamental gardens; and the sun casts dappled shade on the grass from oak, spruce and beech trees, scattered across 52 hectares […]

mix_items.title: Why I sent my archive of nature’s sounds to France (commentary)
mix_items.summary: It is a peculiar irony: as technology reaches ever deeper into Earth’s living systems, the primal sonic expressions of the natural world—wind, water, leaf, and creature—have never been more imperiled. Soundscape ecology rests on a simple conviction: the collective voices of the nonhuman world are not only eloquent, but essential. Recorded and preserved over time, […]

mix_items.title: US public lands tracker highlights the collective impact of Trump policies
mix_items.summary: In his second term as the U.S. president, Donald Trump has taken actions to remove protections from at least 34.8 million hectares (86 million acres) of public lands, according to the advocacy group Center for American Progress. The nonprofit Conservation Lands Foundation (CLF) recently catalogued 12 such policy actions in its newly released Public Lands […]

mix_items.title: Cyclone batters India’s eastern coast, killing 3 and damaging homes and farmland
mix_items.summary: KAKINADA, India (AP) — A powerful cyclone battered India ’s Andhra Pradesh state on Wednesday, killing at least three people and damaging homes and farmland after authorities evacuated tens of thousands of people, officials said. Cyclone Arnab made landfall early Wednesday as a very severe cyclonic storm before weakening to a severe cyclonic storm as […]

mix_items.title: Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years
mix_items.summary: Switzerland’s glaciers are disappearing at an alarming rate, losing more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Some of the country’s most famous glaciers experienced their worst melting on record, while several smaller glaciers vanished completely. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in Japan's 7,300-year-old volcanic apocalypse
mix_items.summary: A catastrophic volcanic eruption 7,300 years ago devastated Japan, but new research reveals that its impact on prehistoric populations was far more complex than previously believed. While some communities disappeared or declined, others unexpectedly flourished as survivors migrated, adapted, and found new ways to thrive.

mix_items.title: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
mix_items.summary: Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.

mix_items.title: Europe's new Sentinel-3C satellite just sent back spectacular images of Earth
mix_items.summary: Europe's Sentinel-3C satellite has returned breathtaking images of Earth just two weeks after launch, revealing the snowy Alps, frozen Arctic islands, and brilliant turquoise Caribbean waters. Its first measurements also show promising results for tracking rising seas, melting ice sheets, and other changes reshaping our planet.

mix_items.title: Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
mix_items.summary: Scientists may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth maintained enough oxygen to support life. Ancient rocks reveal that phosphorus recycling in the oceans created a self-sustaining cycle that helped keep oxygen levels high, even as the planet underwent dramatic environmental changes. The discovery challenges assumptions about Earth's early atmosphere and raises new questions about why complex life took so long to emerge.

mix_items.title: Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
mix_items.summary: The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. Scientists discovered that these changes in the genome's 3D structure may have helped drive the evolution of their unusually complex nervous systems.
